cheatSheet.oneLiner: Vectors, projectile motion, and uniform circular motion — 2D kinematics for NEET.
mustKnowBullets: Scalars have magnitude only; vectors have magnitude and direction.
Vector addition: parallelogram / triangle law; resolve into components.
A · B = AB cosθ; A × B = AB sinθ n̂ (right-hand rule).
Projectile: ax=0, ay=−g; R = (u² sin2θ)/g; H = (u² sin²θ)/(2g); T = (2u sinθ)/g.
Maximum range on level ground at θ = 45°.
Uniform circular motion: a = v²/r toward centre; ω = 2π/T; v = ωr.
Relative velocity in plane: v_AB = v_A − v_B.
Position, velocity, acceleration are vectors; use unit vectors î, ĵ.

highlights.text: Quantity with magnitude only (mass, time, distance).
Scalars have magnitude only; vectors have magnitude and direction.
Vector addition: parallelogram / triangle law; resolve into components.
A · B = AB cosθ; A × B = AB sinθ n̂ (right-hand rule).
Apply sign convention and assumptions before substituting.
Vectors, projectile motion, and uniform circular motion — 2D kinematics for NEET.
For two vectors A and B with an angle θ between them, the resultant R = A + B has magnitude R = √(A²+B²+2AB cosθ), with direction given by tanα = B sinθ/(A+B cosθ) (angle α measured from A).
highlights.whyItMatters: The Law of Cosines / Law of Sines derivation for vector addition — one of the single most frequently tested vector formulas in NEET, used for combining any two forces/velocities/displacements at an angle.

highlights.text: A null (zero) vector is a vector with zero magnitude; its direction cannot be specified. A − A = 0. Key properties: A + 0 = A, and 0·A = 0.
highlights.whyItMatters: Frequently tested conceptual/assertion-reason point — e.g. displacement is a null vector for a round trip.

highlights.text: Motion in a plane (2D) can always be treated as the superposition of two independent, simultaneous one-dimensional motions along two perpendicular directions.
highlights.whyItMatters: The key simplification behind projectile motion — horizontal and vertical motions are analysed completely separately.

highlights.text: Projectile range is maximum when the projection angle θ₀=45°. Ranges are EQUAL for two complementary projection angles (θ and 90°−θ) launched at the same speed, since sin2θ is the same for both.
highlights.whyItMatters: A very frequently tested pair of facts — e.g. 30° and 60° launches give the same range.

formulas.name: Resultant of two vectors (Law of Cosines / Sines)
formulas.plain: resultant magnitude from the law of cosines; direction from the law of sines/tangent relation

symbols.meaning: angle between vectors A and B
angle the resultant R makes with vector A

formulas.whenToUse: Combining any two vectors (forces, velocities, displacements) given their magnitudes and the angle between them — the analytical alternative to drawing a parallelogram.
commonMistakes: Using θ as the angle between the vectors' TAILS when they're drawn head-to-tail (triangle method) instead of tails-together (parallelogram method) — be consistent about which angle is θ.
Forgetting the direction formula gives the angle from vector A specifically, not from some fixed axis.

questionPatterns.patternName: Find resultant magnitude and direction given two vectors and the angle between them
questionPatterns.howToInterpret: Identify A, B and θ; substitute directly into both formulas.
questionPatterns.howItConnectsToFormula: R=√(A²+B²+2AB cosθ) for magnitude, tanα for direction relative to A.
questionPatterns.exampleStem: Two forces of 3 N and 4 N act on a body at an angle of 90° to each other. Find the magnitude and direction of the resultant.

questionPatterns.howToInterpret: R is maximum (=A+B) when θ=0° (same direction) and minimum (=|A−B|) when θ=180° (opposite directions).
questionPatterns.howItConnectsToFormula: Substitute θ=0° or θ=180° into the cosine formula to verify these limits.
questionPatterns.exampleStem: Two vectors of magnitude 5 and 12 units — what are the maximum and minimum possible magnitudes of their resultant?

formulas.audioScript: This formula is just the law of cosines applied to the vector triangle — it lets you find the exact resultant of two vectors at any angle without needing to draw anything, and the companion direction formula tells you exactly which way that resultant points relative to the first vector.

stages.question: Two forces of 3 N and 4 N act on a body at right angles (90°) to each other. Find the magnitude of the resultant force.
stages.interpretation: Direct application of the law-of-cosines resultant formula, with θ=90° simplifying cosθ to 0.
solutionSteps: θ=90°, so cosθ=0, and the formula reduces to R=√(A²+B²)

flashcards.audioScript: At exactly 90 degrees, the cosine term vanishes completely and the law of cosines collapses into the simple Pythagorean theorem — this is why perpendicular vectors are the easiest case to combine.
